name: Earl Warren
kicker: Chief Justice, 1953–1969 · Wrote the 1954 ruling against school segregation
briefing: Earl Warren was a California district attorney, attorney general, and three-term governor before President Dwight Eisenhower made him Chief Justice in 1953. His Court struck down school segregation in _Brown v. Board of Education_, ruled that states must provide lawyers to criminal defendants who cannot afford them, and required the “Miranda warnings” that police read to suspects. He also led the commission that investigated President John F. Kennedy’s assassination.
answerHtml: Earl Warren (prompt on Earl; do not accept “Warren Burger” or “Warren G. Harding”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: This man had never been a judge before joining the Supreme Court; earlier, he spent fourteen years as district attorney of Alameda [“al-uh-MEE-duh”] County, which includes Oakland, and in 1938 he was elected his state’s attorney general.
tossups.r: He later served as governor of California. For 10 points, name this Chief Justice who wrote the unanimous _Brown v. Board of Education_ opinion.

tossups.p: As California’s attorney general in 1942, this man testified to a congressional committee in favor of the forced removal of Japanese Americans from the West Coast, a stand he wrote in his memoirs that he deeply regretted.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this man who later became governor of California and Chief Justice of the United States.

tossups.p: In 1946, thanks to California’s “cross-filing” system, this Republican governor won both his own party’s primary and the Democratic primary for governor, so he faced no major-party opponent that fall. Four years earlier, he had unseated Democratic governor Culbert Olson.
tossups.r: In 1948, he was Thomas Dewey’s running mate. For 10 points, name this man who became Chief Justice in 1953.

tossups.p: After a federal court ruled in _Mendez v. Westminster_ that Mexican American children could not be segregated in Orange County schools, this governor signed a 1947 law repealing California’s remaining school segregation laws.
tossups.r: Seven years later, he wrote the _Brown v. Board of Education_ opinion as Chief Justice. For 10 points, name this California governor.

tossups.p: This man joined the Supreme Court through a recess appointment in October 1953, after Chief Justice Fred Vinson died while a major school case was still undecided. He then worked to make sure that case was decided without any dissent.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Chief Justice who wrote that “separate educational facilities are inherently unequal.”

tossups.p: In a 1955 follow-up ruling, this Chief Justice ordered that public schools be desegregated “with all deliberate speed.” On the same day as his most famous decision, he also wrote _Bolling v. Sharpe_, which struck down school segregation in Washington, D.C.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Chief Justice who wrote the unanimous 1954 _Brown v. Board of Education_ opinion.

tossups.p: In _Reynolds v. Sims_, this justice wrote that “legislators represent people, not trees or acres,” ruling in 1964 that state legislative districts must have roughly equal populations, a principle often summed up as “one person, one vote.”
tossups.r: He also wrote the majority opinion in _Miranda v. Arizona_. For 10 points, name this Chief Justice from 1953 to 1969.

tossups.p: This Chief Justice wrote a 5–4 majority opinion requiring police to tell suspects in custody, before questioning them, that they have the right to remain silent and the right to a lawyer. Statements taken without those warnings, he wrote, cannot be used as evidence at trial.
tossups.r: That 1966 case was _Miranda v. Arizona_. For 10 points, name this man, who also led the commission that investigated John F. Kennedy’s assassination.

tossups.p: Future president Gerald Ford served as a member, and future senator Arlen Specter worked as a lawyer, for a commission led by this man, which Lyndon Johnson created a week after a November 1963 assassination.
tossups.r: In 1964, it concluded that Lee Harvey Oswald had acted alone in killing John F. Kennedy. For 10 points, name this Chief Justice.

tossups.p: In _Trop v. Dulles_, this justice wrote that taking away a wartime deserter’s citizenship was a cruel and unusual punishment, and that the Eighth Amendment “must draw its meaning from the evolving standards of decency that mark the progress of a maturing society.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Chief Justice, a former governor of California, who served from 1953 to 1969.

tossups.p: In 1967, this Chief Justice wrote the unanimous opinion in _Loving v. Virginia_, striking down state laws that banned marriage between people of different races. The case was brought by a Virginia couple, Richard and Mildred Loving.
tossups.r: Thirteen years earlier, he had written the unanimous _Brown v. Board of Education_ decision. For 10 points, name this Chief Justice.

tossups.p: This man was born in Los Angeles in 1891, the son of a Norwegian immigrant who worked for the railroad, and he grew up in Bakersfield before earning a law degree at the University of California, Berkeley.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this three-term governor of California who became Chief Justice in 1953.

tossups.p: When this man announced his retirement in 1968, Lyndon Johnson nominated Justice Abe Fortas to replace him, but Fortas’s nomination stalled in the Senate, and Richard Nixon chose a different successor the next year.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Chief Justice who led the Supreme Court from 1953 to 1969.

tossups.p: This Chief Justice’s Court ruled unanimously that Clarence Gideon, a Florida prisoner who had mailed the justices a handwritten petition, had a right to a lawyer even though he could not afford one.
tossups.r: That 1963 case was _Gideon v. Wainwright_. For 10 points, name this Chief Justice whose Court also decided _Miranda v. Arizona_.

tossups.p: In _Mapp v. Ohio_, this Chief Justice’s Court ruled in 1961 that evidence gathered in an illegal search cannot be used in state courts, applying the “exclusionary rule” to the states. That case began when police searched Dollree Mapp’s home in Cleveland.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Chief Justice, who also led the investigation of John F. Kennedy’s assassination.

clues.t: Chief Justice of the United States (1953–1969), appointed by Dwight Eisenhower
Wrote the unanimous _Brown v. Board of Education_ opinion (1954): “separate educational facilities are inherently unequal”
Led the commission on John F. Kennedy’s assassination, which concluded in 1964 that Lee Harvey Oswald acted alone
Governor of California (1943–1953), elected three times
Wrote the 5–4 _Miranda v. Arizona_ opinion (1966): police must warn suspects of the right to remain silent and to a lawyer
_Gideon v. Wainwright_ (1963): his Court ruled that states must provide lawyers to defendants who cannot afford one
_Reynolds v. Sims_ (1964): “legislators represent people, not trees or acres” (“one person, one vote”)
1948 Republican nominee for vice president, running with Thomas Dewey
As California’s attorney general, he supported the forced removal of Japanese Americans in 1942, which he later said he deeply regretted
Wrote the unanimous _Loving v. Virginia_ opinion (1967), striking down laws banning marriage between people of different races
Lyndon Johnson created his commission in November 1963; Gerald Ford was a member and Arlen Specter a lawyer for it
Got a recess appointment after Chief Justice Fred Vinson died (1953), then worked to make the _Brown_ decision unanimous
_Mapp v. Ohio_ (1961): his Court applied the exclusionary rule (no illegally found evidence) to the states
_Trop v. Dulles_ (1958): wrote that the Eighth Amendment draws its meaning from “evolving standards of decency”
District attorney of Alameda County, which includes Oakland (1925–1939); elected state attorney general in 1938
Won both the Republican and Democratic primaries for governor in 1946 (cross-filing); first elected in 1942 over Culbert Olson
Signed a 1947 law ending school segregation in California after _Mendez v. Westminster_
Born in Los Angeles (1891), son of a Norwegian immigrant railroad worker; grew up in Bakersfield; law degree from Berkeley
_Brown II_ (1955): desegregate “with all deliberate speed”; also wrote _Bolling v. Sharpe_ (1954) on Washington, D.C., schools
After he announced his retirement (1968), Abe Fortas’s nomination to replace him stalled; Richard Nixon chose a successor in 1969
Had never been a judge before becoming Chief Justice
Clarence Gideon mailed the justices a handwritten petition from a Florida prison

trap.title: Which Warren?
trap.body: Three famous Warrens show up in quiz bowl. Earl Warren was Chief Justice from 1953 to 1969; Warren Burger, whose full name was Warren Earl Burger, replaced him in 1969; and Warren G. Harding was the 29th president (1921–1923). Real answer lines for this man do not accept Burger or Harding. Questions about “this commission” or “this court” want the Warren Commission or the Warren Court, not just his name.
trap.fix: Earl Warren clues: governor of California, _Brown v. Board_, _Miranda_, _Gideon_, and the Kennedy assassination commission. Burger clues: Richard Nixon appointed him, and he wrote _United States v. Nixon_ (1974), the Watergate tapes case. Harding clues: the Teapot Dome scandal and a “return to normalcy.”
trap.line: Real answer line: Earl Warren (do not accept “Warren Burger” or “Warren G. Harding”)
